passage:
“Anirban, I redid the client summary last night,” Sabina said, dropping the printout on his desk.
“Was it wrong?”
“Not wrong. Just slow to read. It's faster if I do it myself. Explaining it would take longer.”
“I could have fixed it.”
“Then I'd have had to review it. This way it's done.” Sabina rubbed her eyes. “I'll take the vendor report as well.”
“You already have six reports.”
“I know. It's fine.”
Anirban looked at the pile on her desk, then at his own, almost empty. Nobody had shown him how to write these summaries, and he no longer asked.
Sabina's light was still on at nine.

qa.q: What did Sabina redo the night before?
qa.a: Sabina redid the client summary.

qa.q: Why does Sabina say she will do the work herself?
qa.a: Sabina feels it is faster and safer than explaining, and worries about the time review would take.

qa.q: What is the cost of Sabina's approach, and what could change it?
qa.a: Sabina's workload keeps growing and Anirban never learns; Sabina could explain one summary once and let Anirban try before redoing anything.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel looking at his own almost empty desk?
qa.a: Anirban may feel unneeded and a bit discouraged, with no chance to learn, and has stopped asking questions.

grounding: Someone newly in charge redoes a team member's work personally because it feels faster and safer than explaining.

passage:
When I became a team lead, I decided I was the safest pair of hands. Sachin would submit the weekly sheet and I would quietly rewrite it at night, because explaining what was wrong took thirty minutes and fixing it took ten. I told myself it was efficiency. In the first month I was leaving at nine every day. In the second month I had a headache most mornings. Sachin, meanwhile, made the same mistakes each week, because nobody had ever shown him the reason for them. The weekly sheets were perfect and the team learned nothing. Looking back, what surprised me was how virtuous I felt, tired and indispensable, when I was really just afraid of the mess.
— Nandini

qa.q: What time was Nandini leaving in the first month?
qa.a: In the first month Nandini was leaving at nine every day.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel while rewriting Sachin's sheets at night?
qa.a: Nandini felt virtuous, tired and indispensable, but underneath was afraid of the mess.

qa.q: What price did the shortcut cost Nandini and the team?
qa.a: Nandini worked late and had headaches, and Sachin never learned, so the same mistakes repeated each week.

qa.q: What might Sachin have thought about the weekly sheet coming back perfect?
qa.a: Sachin probably saw the sheet fixed without any explanation, so may have felt unsure why it was wrong, and had no way to improve.

grounding: A new team lead redoes tasks because it feels faster, at the cost of a growing personal workload and a team that never learns.

passage: Eshaan, twenty-five, had just been made supervisor at the milk cooperative in a small town near Anand. He had three staff under him, including Yash, who had joined a month ago. Each evening the collection records had to be checked and sent to the district office. Yash made mistakes the first time, so Eshaan started doing the records himself. It took him ninety minutes. Then he did the stock sheet himself too, and the farmers' payment list. By the end of the month he was leaving at ten, eyes stinging, while Yash sat idle by six. One evening Yash asked quietly, "Don't you trust me with anything?" Eshaan had no answer. The next day he sat with Yash and walked him through the records.

qa.q: How long did the evening records take Eshaan?
qa.a: It took him ninety minutes.

qa.q: What was Eshaan feeling when Yash asked if he was trusted?
qa.a: He was caught off guard and uncomfortable, with no answer, realising his habit looked like distrust.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what did Eshaan do to fix it?
qa.a: Doing every task himself swelled his workload and left Yash idle and untrained; he fixed it by walking Yash through the records.

qa.q: How does Yash feel sitting idle by six?
qa.a: Yash feels unused and doubted, which is why Yash quietly asks about being trusted with anything.

grounding: Shows a new supervisor redoing tasks himself because it feels faster, growing his workload and leaving his team unskilled.

passage: Jana had been promoted to lead a small editing team at a publishing house in Prague. When the first manuscript came back from Ingrid with small errors, Jana corrected it herself. It was quicker than writing notes. The next one, she simply didn't send to Ingrid at all. By spring Jana was editing four books alone, working weekends, and her team was handling only emails. At the monthly review, her director asked why the team's skills hadn't grown. Jana opened her mouth to defend herself and realised he was right. She booked an hour with Ingrid the next Monday, not to fix a manuscript, but to show her how she edits.

qa.q: How many books was Jana editing alone by spring?
qa.a: Jana was editing four books alone.

qa.q: What did Jana feel when the director asked about the team's skills?
qa.a: She felt defensive at first, then uncomfortable as she realised he was right.

qa.q: What was Jana's hour with Ingrid meant to change?
qa.a: It was meant to teach Ingrid how Jana edits, so the work can be shared instead of all falling on Jana.

qa.q: How might Ingrid have felt when manuscripts stopped coming to her?
qa.a: Ingrid might have felt sidelined and unsure, left with only emails and no chance to learn.

grounding: Shows a new team lead redoing her team's work herself, which grows her workload and leaves the team unskilled.

passage: In her first month as shift lead at the Andheri branch library, Ira had a habit. Avni would shelve the new arrivals, and after closing Ira would quietly re-shelve half of them. Avni would draft the poster for Saturday's story hour, and Ira would redo it at home because explaining the font rules took longer. "Faster if I just do it," she told herself, eating dinner at the desk at nine. By the fourth week, Ira was the only one who knew how to log inter-branch loans, set up the story-hour projector or file the monthly count. Then, one Saturday morning, her train was stuck for three hours. Twenty children and their parents waited in the reading room while Avni tried the projector cables one by one. When Ira arrived, Avni said quietly, "I didn't know how. You never let me."

qa.q: How long was Ira's train stuck on Saturday morning?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: Why did Ira keep redoing Avni's work?
qa.a: Ira felt uneasy trusting the work to someone else and told herself it was faster, so redoing it felt safer than explaining.

qa.q: What could Ira do differently from Monday?
qa.a: Ira could teach Avni the projector, the loan log and the monthly count one at a time and let Avni's poster stand, so the branch works without her.

qa.q: How does Avni feel about the way Ira has been working?
qa.a: Avni feels hurt and discouraged, left unable to help and then blamed in front of families, which comes out in "You never let me."

grounding: Shows a new lead who redoes tasks herself because it feels quicker, piling up her own workload while her colleague never learns.
